title: What should you ask first in a market entry case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a market entry case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Market entry cases ask a yes or no question: should the client go in? Here is how to get to a clear answer.
body:
The first question to ask

What is the goal, and over what time frame?

How to build your structure

  • Is the market attractive? (size and growth, margins, barriers to entry)
  • Can we win? (competitors, customer needs, our edge)
  • Will it pay? (revenue, costs, upfront investment, payback)
  • Can we pull it off? (capabilities we lack, build / partner / buy, timing and pilot, risks)

The trap most people fall into

Forgetting entry mode and timing; no pilot.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the market entry framework.

Two prompts to try

Should a supermarket invest in vertical farms to grow salad near its stores?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Demand for fresh local salad; Price premium shoppers pay
  • Economics: Cost per kg vs buying from growers; Energy prices
  • Capability: Running farms vs partnering; Technology risk
  • Strategic value: Less waste, fresher produce; Supply security, carbon

Where to start: Cost per kg, especially energy, vs buying from growers.

The trap: Being won over by the story before checking energy costs.

Mini case: a coffee chain considers another country

A UK chain wants to enter a new market and expects each shop to generate £600,000 of yearly sales. At a 15% operating margin, one mature shop would contribute £90,000 of operating profit. If opening a shop requires £450,000 of investment, simple operating-profit payback is five years, ignoring ramp-up, tax and the cost of capital.

The calculation is only the beginning. Ask how many locations meet the required footfall and rental economics, whether the brand can command the assumed price, and whether reliable suppliers exist. A ten-store rollout may need £4.5 million of initial capital before working capital and market-entry overhead.

Recommend a pilot if uncertainty is high: two locations, clear customer and unit-economics targets, and a stop/go decision after enough trading data. Compare the opportunity with improving current stores or franchising instead. "The market is growing" is not sufficient evidence that this client can enter profitably.
